links.outcome: Head-to-head comparison of two FDA-cleared mammography AIs on same data for operational safety
links.effect: AI #1 had higher AUC (0.928 vs 0.882), but at alpha=100% AI #2 ruled out 290 true negatives (29.0%) vs 167 (16.7%) for AI #1; difference 123 cases (95% CI 87.0–150.0).
links.quote: This represents a substantial improvement over AI #1, which cleared only 167 cases (16.7% of the cohort), with a difference of 123 cases in the Rule-out Safe Zone in favor of AI #2 (95% confidence interval: 87.0–150.0).

links.outcome: Whether AUC alone versus reliability-based operational metrics distinguishes model safety
links.effect: Models with nearly identical AUC 0.960 had Gray Zone Areas of 0.709 vs 0.344; the higher-AUC FDA-cleared model was less safe for high-confidence rule-out.
links.quote: This result shows that the AUC can be misleading and that models should be evaluated for their operational safety to understand their true clinical utility.

links.outcome: Deriving decision thresholds from clinician-defined PPV/NPV targets or utility maximization
links.effect: Different policies (balanced, high-precision referral, high-volume screening, strictly non-negligent, minimize FP harm) produced different thresholds and Gray Zone workloads on the same model; demonstrated, not tested against a comparator.
links.quote: Beyond direct rules, the framework navigates more complex scenarios by maximizing a clinical utility function that weighs the nuanced costs of errors against the benefits of correct decisions.

links.outcome: Human radiologist accuracy within AI-defined Safe Zones, including over-calling in Rule-out zone
links.effect: In the Rule-out Safe Zone human accuracy was at its lowest due to high false-positive rate; radiologists frequently flagged AI-identified safe cases as suspicious.
links.quote: Here, where the AI was most confident that cases were low-risk (e.g., α ⁻ = 100%), human accuracy was paradoxically at its lowest.

links.effect: AI #1 had higher AUC than AI #2 (0.928 vs. 0.882) but at α=100% cleared 167 cases (16.7%) versus AI #2's 290 (29.0%).
links.quote: Although AI Solution #1 demonstrated a higher AUC than AI Solution #2 (0.928 vs. 0.882; Fig. 3a , b ), this advantage translated to better operational efficiency only for less stringent tasks, as evidenced by its more rapid Gray Zone reduction at moderate safety levels ( α < 95%; Fig. 3c ).

links.effect: At α=100%, AI #2 ruled out 290 true negatives (29.0%) versus AI #1's 167 (16.7%); difference 123 cases (95% CI: 87.0–150.0).
links.quote: This represents a substantial improvement over AI #1, which cleared only 167 cases (16.7% of the cohort), with a difference of 123 cases in the Rule-out Safe Zone in favor of AI #2 (95% confidence interval: 87.0–150.0).

links.effect: For a missed-cancer-is-unacceptable policy, target 100% NPV eliminated any rule-out and deferred all but most certain positives to human review.
links.quote: Faced with a ‘strictly non-negligent’ policy where missing a cancer is unacceptable (Fig. 5e ), the optimal strategy becomes highly conservative: to achieve the target of 100% NPV, the AI eliminates its ability to rule out any case, deferring all but the most certain positive calls to human review.

links.effect: At α=100%, AI #2 ruled out 163 cases that AI #1 left in its uncertain Gray Zone.
links.quote: Crucially, 163 of the cases that AI #1 left in its uncertain Gray Zone were confidently ruled out by AI #2 (Fig. 3d ).

links.effect: Across 1%–40% prevalence, two high-performing AI solutions showed vastly different operational stability profiles.
links.quote: Our prevalence simulation analysis (see Supplementary Note 1 ) provides a clear example, demonstrating how two high-performing AI solutions respond in vastly different ways to shifts in epidemiological context.

links.outcome: Operational safety versus AUC ranking in cancer screening AI
links.effect: AI Solution #1 had higher AUC (0.928 vs 0.882), but AI #2 ruled out 123 more true negatives (290 vs 167; 95% CI: 87.0-150.0) at maximal safety (α = 100%).
links.quote: A comparison of two FDA-cleared mammography AIs shows a notable performance reversal: the model with superior statistical performance was not the most operationally robust for high-confidence screening.
